query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor boron doping during processing will enhance the grain boundary cohesion of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, thereby increasing its load-bearing integrity while preserving its large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operating regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in its undoped form exhibits strong caloric effects but suffers from poor load-bearing integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small concentration of boron as a dopant during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: The alloy is tested under conditions typical for solid refrigeration including applied magnetic or pressure fields, with operating temperatures ranging from room temperature to cryogenic levels and under mechanical loading relevant to refrigeration device operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion via boron segregation, which can reduce grain-boundary energy and suppress crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms, when added in minor amounts, are expected to migrate to and segregate at the grain boundaries during solidification and subsequent processing. This segregation strengthens the binding between grains without significantly altering the microstructural phases responsible for the caloric response, thus preserving the functional performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The doped alloy should exhibit a measurable increase in fracture toughness and overall load-bearing integrity, with little to no degradation in its caloric performance under applied fields and pressure.
generation.baseline: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which has excellent caloric response but low fracture toughness and poor resistance to crack propagation.
generation.boundary: The effects are expected under standard refrigeration operational fields (magnetic or pressure) and across the temperature and mechanical loading ranges typical for such applications. The intervention should not compromise phase stability or the caloric mechanism within these regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the improvement in mechanical integrity and the exact retention of caloric performance remain to be determined; potential interactions between boron and other alloying elements could have unforeseen secondary effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with a minor concentration of boron added during processing, and a control set without boron. Process both sets under identical conditions to form (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloys. Conduct standardized mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness or bending tests) and caloric performance measurements (e.g., isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change under applied fields) for each set under identical operational regimes.
measurements: Fracture toughness (using J-integral and/or stress intensity factor methods)
Load-bearing tests (e.g., bending or compression tests to monitor crack initiation and propagation)
Caloric effect measurements (quantifying isothermal entropy changes or temperature changes)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM to verify boron segregation at grain boundaries)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., less than a 10% increase in fracture toughness or load-bearing capacity) or if there is a measurable degradation (e.g., more than a 5% drop) in the caloric response compared to the undoped control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Microhardness behavior of sintered Ni–Al–Ti–Mn–Co–Fe–Cr HEA
cited_evidence.text: The precipitation of the coarse NiAl eutectic phase along the grain boundaries was caused to dissolve during the sintering process by the nucleation of micro-sized Ti–Mn–Co–Fe–Cr particles in the solid solution of Ni–Al–Ti–Mn–Co–Fe–Cr and form homogenized, evenly distributed fine particles at the borders. The strengthening of the HEA was made possible by this phase of refinement [, , ]. Thus, the increased grain size brought on by the populated coarse NiAl eutectic phase (BCC B2 phase) accounts for the unalloyed NiAl's reduced hardness.

The rapid ultrahigh-temperature sintering technique not only can create the eutectic liquid phase for the fast densification but also helps improve the interfaces between the boron carbide and HEB. Coherent interface can be found in the composite, as shown in Fig. 5A. The HRTEM image (Fig. 5B) and SAEDs indicate that the boron carbide and HEB grains can have coherent interfaces, as the zone axis [010] of B13C2 is parallel to the [211¯] zone axis of HEB and the (101) plane of boron carbide is coherent with the (1¯20) plane of HEB. This coherent structure indicates that the HEB surface provides nucleation sites that guide the grain growth of the boron carbide, which can further improve the interfacial binding between the two components. We further conducted Vickers hardness experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of this eutectic liquid–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering approach (Fig. 5C). We used the same ultrahigh-temperature sintering approach to synthesize a HEB without boron carbide and intergranular ZrB12 phases (detailed characterization can be found in fig. S13).
